title: Exponential Growth and Decay
intro: Many real quantities change by a fixed percentage each period — populations, investments, radioactive material. This chapter covers growth and decay models, population and financial applications, and reading a model’s rate. Read each topic, work the problems with the hint ladder, then take the 8-question topic test.

topics.name: Growth Models
topics.details: A quantity that grows by a fixed percentage each period follows A = P(1 + r)^t, where P is the starting amount, r the growth rate as a decimal, and t the number of periods. A base (1 + r) greater than 1 signals growth. For 500 growing 20% per period, after 2 periods it is 500(1.2)² = 500 × 1.44 = 720. Convert the percent to a decimal, add 1, raise to the number of periods, and multiply by the start. The exponent counts periods, not years unless stated. The SAT keeps the exponent small so the arithmetic is exact and tests whether you set up (1 + r)^t correctly.

topics.name: Decay Models
topics.details: A quantity that shrinks by a fixed percentage each period follows A = P(1 − r)^t, the mirror of growth. The base (1 − r) lies between 0 and 1, which signals decay. For 800 decaying 20% per period, after 2 periods it is 800(0.8)² = 800 × 0.64 = 512. Subtract the rate from 1 first, then raise to the number of periods and multiply by the start. Decay appears in depreciation, cooling and half-life style problems. The most common error is forgetting to subtract from 1 (using 0.2 instead of 0.8). The SAT tests setting up (1 − r)^t and telling decay from growth by the base.

topics.name: Population Models
topics.details: Populations that grow by a steady percentage each year are a classic application of A = P(1 + r)^t, with P the starting population, r the annual growth rate as a decimal, and t the number of years. A town of 10,000 growing 20% per year has 10,000(1.2)² = 14,400 after 2 years. The model assumes a constant percentage rate, so each year’s increase is larger than the last (it compounds). Set up (1 + r)^t exactly as with general growth, reading “per year” as the period. The SAT uses small year counts so the result is exact, and may ask you to interpret the base or rate in context.

A town of 5,000 grows 10% per year. After 2 years?
A colony of 2,000 grows 50% per year. After 2 years?
In P = 8000(1.1)^t, what is the starting population?

topics.name: Financial Applications
topics.details: Money invested at compound interest grows exponentially: A = P(1 + r)^t, with P the principal, r the annual rate as a decimal, and t the number of years. This is the same formula as population growth applied to dollars. For $1,000 at 20% compounded annually for 2 years, A = 1000(1.2)² = $1,440. The interest earned is the final amount minus the principal. Compounding means interest earns interest, so the total exceeds simple interest over the same period. Set up (1 + r)^t carefully and decide whether the question wants the total amount or just the interest. The SAT keeps the rates and years clean.
